transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. ____. What brings you in today?

Well, they sent me here because of something that happened at the station. I was... I kept moving the airway bags into a pattern. I just knew it was the right way to do it, and I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud while I set them up. 

My lieutenant told me to stop and step away, but I wouldn't. I couldn't, really. It felt like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence. So, that's why they brought me in.
When you were arranging the bags and repeating the numbers, did you believe something bad would actually happen if you didn’t do it?

Yeah, exactly. Like I was saying, I really felt like the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence. It wasn't just a passing thought, I just knew that pattern was right and I had to finish it. That's why I wouldn't step away when my lieutenant told me to stop. I had to keep moving the airway bags into that exact arrangement and keep repeating those dispatch numbers out loud, or else everything would just... go bad. I couldn't just leave it undone.
At the time, did you think this belief might be unreasonable or excessive?

No, I... I didn't think it was unreasonable at all. It just felt like a fact. I wasn't really stopping to think if it was excessive or if it made sense to anybody else. I just... I just knew I had to do it.
Did you think that other people would see this as odd or not true?

I didn't really think about what other people would see. I wasn't paying attention to them or what they thought about it. I was just focused on the bags and the numbers. It didn't cross my mind to wonder if it looked odd to anyone else.
At any point, did you think there was a real possibility that this belief could be wrong?
No, I... I never thought it could be wrong. It didn't even occur to me to question it. It was just... what had to happen. I didn't doubt it for a second.
Looking back now, do you think that belief was unreasonable?

I don't really know. I mean... even sitting here now, it still feels like it was real. I don't look back and think it was unreasonable. It just... it still seems like it was exactly what I needed to do at the time.
Did you ever have any actual evidence that something bad would happen if you did not arrange the bags that way?

No, I didn't have proof, like... something you could hold or see. But I knew it. That's why they sent me here. At the station, I just kept moving the airway bags into the pattern I knew was right. I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud, over and over. My lieutenant told me to stop and step away, but I wouldn't. I couldn't. It felt like... if I broke the sequence, the whole ambulance bay would just go bad. I didn't need evidence, I just felt it.
Do you now see this belief as something that was definitely true, or as something that might have been a false alarm?

I... I still see it as something that was definitely true. I don't think it was a false alarm. Like I was saying, it still feels completely real to me even right now. I know my lieutenant and the doctors don't see it that way, but... no, to me, it wasn't a false alarm. It was true.
Have you ever heard, seen, or otherwise sensed things that other people around you could not?

No, I haven't. I mean... I know what you're asking, like hearing voices or seeing things that aren't there. But no, I don't get anything like that. It's just... the feelings I get about the patterns and the numbers. That's all it is. I don't hear anyone talking to me or see anything strange.
Do you ever recognize that these thoughts or rituals might be coming from your own mind and not be true?

No, I don't. I mean... I know that's what everyone here keeps telling me, but no. I don't sit back and think it's just my mind playing tricks on me. The patterns and the rules with the bags, they're real. It's not just my imagination making things up. I really don't see it as something that isn't true.
Do the people around you who share your background or work setting also believe that arranging the bags and repeating the numbers this way is necessary?

No, they don't. My partner on the ambulance, the other EMTs at the station... they definitely don't think it's necessary. They just kind of... they look at me strange when I do it, or tell me to hurry up. Nobody else arranges the jump bags that way or does the numbers. It's really just me.
Has this belief or practice been something that is commonly accepted in your family, community, or work culture?

No, it's not. Like I was just saying about work, the other EMTs don't do it. And my family... no, they don't do anything like this either. It's not a religious thing or some tradition I was taught growing up. It's just... it's just what I have to do.
When you were doing the arranging and repeating, did it feel unwanted or intrusive to you, or did it feel completely right and in line with what you wanted to do?

It didn't feel unwanted at all. It felt... it felt like exactly what I was supposed to be doing. I mean, they sent me here because of it. At the station, I kept moving the airway bags into this specific pattern that I just knew was right, and I was repeating the dispatch numbers out loud. My lieutenant came over and told me to stop, to step away, but I wouldn't. I couldn't. It felt like... if I broke that sequence, the whole ambulance bay would just go bad. So, no, it didn't feel intrusive. It felt completely necessary.
Do these patterns and number-repeating feel distressing or unwanted to you?

Like I was just saying, no, they aren't unwanted at all. And they don't distress me. It's really the exact opposite. Doing it makes me feel like things are correct... so it just feels like exactly what I need to be doing.

Before you do the patterning or the number-repeating, do you feel driven by a fear or doubt that something bad will happen if you don’t, or does it feel like a fixed belief that it must be done because it is true?

It's definitely a fixed belief. It's not like a doubt or a worry. Like I was just saying about what happened at the station... when I was arranging those airway bags and repeating the dispatch numbers, I didn't do it out of fear. I did it because I just knew it was right. It was a fact. 

That's why I wouldn't step away when my lieutenant told me to stop. I knew for a fact that the whole bay would go bad if I broke the sequence. It wasn't a "what if" kind of thing. So, yeah, I do it because it must be done, because it's true.
Do you try to resist or stop yourself from doing the bag-arranging and number-repeating, or does it feel completely natural to do?

No, I don't try to resist it. It feels completely natural to do. Like I was saying a minute ago, that's the whole reason they sent me here. When I was at the station moving those airway bags into that pattern and saying the dispatch numbers out loud, I wasn't trying to stop myself at all. Even when my lieutenant was standing right there telling me to step away, I wouldn't do it. I just kept going because... well, because breaking the sequence meant the whole bay would go bad. So, no, I don't fight it. It just feels like what I'm supposed to do.
